body:
Meaning of Indo-Islamic architecture

Indo-Islamic architecture refers to architectural traditions that developed in the Indian subcontinent through interaction between local building practices and architectural forms associated with Muslim rulers, merchants, religious communities and craftspeople. Its major expressions include mosques, tombs, minarets, forts, gateways, palaces and formal gardens.

These buildings did not simply reproduce structures from West Asia or Central Asia. Indian builders were already skilled in stone carving, pillared halls, brackets, lintels and ornamental sculpture. New patrons introduced or encouraged forms such as large true arches, prominent domes, monumental gateways and geometrically organised gardens. Architects and artisans combined these elements according to local materials, established skills and regional preferences.

The result was not one uniform style. A mosque in Gujarat could have finely carved pillars and screens resembling local temple craftsmanship, while a mosque in Bengal might use brick and a curved roofline adapted to regional traditions.

Historical development

Interactions involving Muslim communities and building traditions existed in parts of the subcontinent before the establishment of the Delhi Sultanate. However, large-scale construction under Turkish political patronage expanded from the late 12th and early 13th centuries. The rulers of the Delhi Sultanate commissioned mosques, tombs, fortifications and towers that made the new architectural vocabulary increasingly prominent in northern India.

From the 14th and 15th centuries, regional Sultanates developed recognisable styles. Gujarat, Bengal, Jaunpur and Malwa adapted similar architectural requirements in different ways. The Deccan Sultanates developed further regional traditions.

Under the Mughals, especially from Akbar to Shah Jahan, architectural planning became increasingly associated with monumental scale, carefully proportioned buildings, formal gardens, red sandstone, white marble and refined surface decoration.

How architectural styles are classified

StyleMain settingGeneral character
Imperial or Delhi SultanateDelhi and its political centresEarly monumental mosques, arches, towers and tombs
Provincial SultanateGujarat, Bengal, Jaunpur and MalwaAdaptation of Sultanate forms to regional materials and craftsmanship
DeccaniBijapur and Golconda regionsLarge domes, distinctive towers and regional ornament
MughalAgra, Delhi, Fatehpur Sikri and other imperial centresFormal symmetry, gardens, monumental gateways and refined stone decoration

These categories describe broad historical tendencies. They are not rigid divisions: a building may combine features associated with several traditions.

Architecture, religion and political authority

Buildings served practical, religious and political purposes. A congregational mosque accommodated collective prayer; a tomb commemorated a deceased ruler or important person; a fort provided defence and administrative space. Monumental construction also demonstrated the resources and authority of its patron.

Architectural patronage encouraged the movement of artisans and ideas between regions. During Akbar's reign, for example, buildings at Fatehpur Sikri incorporated features associated with the craftsmanship of Gujarat and Malwa.

Indo-Islamic architecture is not defined by the exclusive use of arches and domes. Pillars, beams, carved brackets, regional roof forms and other established Indian elements continued to be used. The combination of techniques is central to understanding the tradition.

Prelims focus

  • Indo-Islamic architecture developed through interaction between local Indian and wider Islamic architectural traditions.
  • Large-scale construction under Turkish political patronage expanded from the late 12th and early 13th centuries.
  • Provincial styles include Gujarat, Bengal, Jaunpur and Malwa.
  • The Deccani style is associated with centres such as Bijapur and Golconda.
  • Mughal architecture drew upon both Central Asian and regional Indian traditions.
  • Trap: The presence of a dome does not automatically make a building Mughal.

[Sources: NCERT, An Introduction to Indian Art, Part I, Class 11, Chapter 8, Some Aspects of Indo-Islamic Architecture, pp. 109–111; NCERT, Our Pasts–II, Class 7, Chapter 5, Rulers and Buildings, pp. 66–72.]

pictures.alt: Builders carve sandstone beside pillared colonnades and a pointed gateway in an early 13th-century Delhi mosque courtyard.
pictures.caption: Architecture in medieval Delhi brought together established Indian building traditions and new architectural forms.

title: The Emergence and Character of Indo-Islamic Architecture in India

body:
Trabeate and arcuate construction

Two important methods of supporting the weight above an opening are the trabeate and arcuate systems.

In trabeate construction, a horizontal beam or lintel rests on vertical supports such as pillars or walls. This system was extensively used in Indian temple architecture and continued to appear in medieval mosques and palaces.

In arcuate construction, an arch carries the weight above an opening and transfers it towards its supporting sides. A properly constructed masonry arch allows a wider opening to be made without a continuous horizontal stone beam.

Corbelled arch and true arch

A corbelled arch is created by arranging horizontal courses of stone so that each successive course projects slightly inward. The opposite sides eventually meet near the top. Although the opening may look arched, the construction is based on projecting masonry rather than the action of a true arch.

A true arch is formed from wedge-shaped blocks called voussoirs. The central wedge-shaped block at the crown is the keystone. The blocks press against one another, transferring the load downward and outward towards supporting piers or walls. Those supports must resist the outward thrust.

The Alai Darwaza, built by Alauddin Khalji in 1311 within Delhi's Qutb complex, is an important example of developed true-arch construction in the Sultanate period.

Domes and their supports

A dome is a curved roof that covers a space. Many prominent Indo-Islamic domes rise above square or rectangular chambers. The principal structural challenge is to provide an appropriate base for a circular dome over a square room.

Two important solutions are:

  • Squinch: An arch or similar construction across the corner of a square chamber. Squinches help transform the square space below into a polygonal base for the dome.
  • Pendentive: A curved triangular supporting surface that helps carry a dome above a square chamber, transferring its load towards the supporting arches and piers.

A double dome has separate inner and outer shells. This allows the exterior dome to appear tall and imposing while the ceiling experienced inside can remain lower and more proportionate to the chamber. Double-dome construction became important in major Mughal tombs.

Minarets and minars

A minaret is a tower commonly associated with a mosque. Traditionally, a minaret could provide an elevated position for the azan, or call to prayer. Monumental minars also expressed the prestige and authority of a patron.

The Qutb Minar in Delhi is a major Sultanate example. Qutbuddin Aibak laid its foundation in 1199 and constructed its first storey. Iltutmish added further storeys, while later rulers undertook repairs and alterations. The surviving monument has 5 storeys and a height of approximately 72.5 m. Its exterior includes red and buff sandstone, projecting balconies, fluting and bands of inscriptions.

Not every minaret belongs to a mosque, and not every tower called a minar served exactly the same purpose. The 4 towers at the corners of the Taj Mahal's platform are part of a monumental tomb composition rather than the defining feature of a congregational mosque.

Arch: curved structural opening. Dome: curved roof covering a space. Minaret: tower commonly associated with a mosque. These terms name different architectural elements, not interchangeable parts of a building.

Prelims focus

  • Trabeate construction uses horizontal beams supported by pillars or walls.
  • A true arch uses voussoirs and a keystone; a corbelled arch uses projecting horizontal courses.
  • Alai Darwaza was built by Alauddin Khalji in 1311.
  • Squinches and pendentives help support domes over square chambers.
  • Qutb Minar was begun by Qutbuddin Aibak in 1199 and later enlarged by Iltutmish.
  • Trap: A corbelled opening can resemble an arch without being a structurally true arch.

[Sources: NCERT, Our Pasts–II, Class 7, Chapter 5, Rulers and Buildings, pp. 60–63; NCERT, An Introduction to Indian Art, Part I, Class 11, Chapter 8, pp. 109, 113–114, and Glossary, pp. 126–130; Archaeological Survey of India, Qutb Minar and its Monuments, monument description, accessed 23 November 2026.]

pictures.alt: Corbelled openings use projecting horizontal courses; true arches use wedge-shaped voussoirs and a crown keystone to carry load towards supporting piers.
pictures.caption: A corbelled opening uses projecting horizontal courses; a true arch uses wedge-shaped blocks and a keystone.

pictures.alt: A square room needs a transition to a dome: squinches arch across corners; pendentives form curved triangular surfaces between arches and dome.
pictures.caption: Squinches and pendentives provide different ways to support a dome above a square chamber.

title: Arches, Domes and Minarets: Forms and Structural Principles

body:
The mosque as a place of prayer

A masjid, or mosque, is a place of Muslim prayer. A Jama Masjid, also called a Jami Masjid or congregational mosque, is intended particularly for collective Friday prayer. Such mosques often have larger courtyards and prayer halls to accommodate a congregation.

One of the most important principles of mosque planning is the qibla, the direction of the Kaaba at Mecca towards which worshippers face. In much of India, the qibla is broadly westward. For this reason, the main prayer hall of many historical Indian mosques occupies the western side of the courtyard.

Identifying the parts of a mosque

TermMeaningFunction
SahnOpen courtyardProvides space for congregation and circulation
LiwanCovered hall or colonnaded spaceProvides sheltered space; the qibla-side hall is used for prayer
MihrabNiche in the qibla wallIndicates the direction of Mecca
MimbarRaised or stepped pulpitUsed for delivering the Friday sermon
Ablution tankWater facility, where providedSupports washing before prayer
MinaretTower, where providedHistorically associated with the call to prayer and monumental expression

These are common elements, not a compulsory list for every mosque. The size and arrangement of buildings differed according to region, period and available resources.

Tombs, mausoleums and dargahs

A maqbara or mausoleum is a building associated with a grave or burial. Monumental tombs were constructed for rulers, members of royal families and other prominent individuals. In some tombs, an ornamental cenotaph appears in the main chamber while the actual grave is in a lower chamber.

A dargah is a shrine associated with the burial place of a Sufi saint. A dargah may include a tomb, prayer areas, courtyards and facilities for visitors. The distinction is based primarily on religious association and function: a royal mausoleum commemorates a ruler or noble, whereas a dargah is connected with veneration of a saint.

Some monumental tombs were placed within gardens. The combination of a tomb, water channels and ordered planting became especially prominent in Mughal architecture.

Other important structures

  • Fort: A defended complex that could contain residences, administrative buildings, stores and water facilities. Agra Fort and the Red Fort in Delhi are important Mughal examples.
  • Sarai: A lodging place for travellers, merchants and their animals, often situated along important routes.
  • Madrasa: An institution or building associated with religious and other learning.
  • Hammam: A bathhouse, sometimes incorporated into palace or other large complexes.
  • Gateway: A prominent entrance that could serve practical, ceremonial and symbolic purposes.

The same architectural vocabulary could appear in several building types. An arch might form a mosque entrance, a palace doorway or a tomb's façade. Therefore, identifying a monument requires attention to both its structural features and its original function.

Prelims focus

  • Jama Masjid means a congregational mosque associated particularly with Friday prayer.
  • The mihrab marks the qibla, or direction of Mecca.
  • The mimbar is the pulpit used for the sermon.
  • The sahn is the open courtyard of a mosque.
  • A maqbara is a tomb or mausoleum; a dargah is associated with a Sufi saint's shrine.
  • Trap: Mihrab and mimbar are different architectural features.

[Sources: NCERT, An Introduction to Indian Art, Part I, Class 11, Chapter 8, pp. 110, 114–115, 124, and Glossary, pp. 127–130; NCERT, Our Pasts–II, Class 7, Chapter 3, The Delhi Sultans, section The Masjid, p. 36.]

pictures.alt: Mosque plan showing the courtyard, surrounding cloisters, western prayer hall, mihrab, mimbar, ablution tank and entrance, with qibla pointing west.
pictures.caption: The principal parts of a typical medieval Indian congregational mosque.

title: Mosques, Tombs and Other Buildings: Understanding Their Plans and Functions

body:
Why decoration matters

Indo-Islamic buildings are recognised not only by their arches, domes and plans but also by the treatment of their surfaces. Carved stone, pierced screens, coloured inlay, calligraphy and repeating patterns were used on walls, gateways, tomb chambers and prayer halls.

Many religious buildings emphasised plant forms, geometry and calligraphy. However, it would be inaccurate to claim that all Indo-Islamic art excluded human or animal figures. Figural imagery also appeared in some secular and courtly settings. The nature of decoration depended on the building's function and patronage.

Arabesque: A flowing ornamental design

An arabesque is an ornamental pattern made from interlacing, flowing lines, tendrils, leaves or stylised flowers. The elements may repeat continuously across a surface.

An arabesque is a type of design, not a particular building material or construction method. It may be carved in stone, moulded in plaster, painted or created through inlay. Curving plant stems that connect flowers and leaves are characteristic examples.

Jali: A perforated screen

A jali is a lattice or screen containing openings cut through the material, often stone or marble. Its design may feature geometric stars, polygons, floral patterns, trees or interlacing forms.

Jalis allow light and air to pass through while partly screening the space behind them. They also produce distinctive patterns of light and shadow. This combination of decoration and function explains their presence in mosques, tombs, windows and palace buildings.

The celebrated Sidi Saiyyed Mosque in Ahmedabad is especially known for stone jalis depicting intertwined branches and the tree of life. The mosque was completed in 1573.

Pietra dura: Coloured-stone inlay

Pietra dura, also called hard-stone inlay, involves fitting pieces of coloured and often semi-precious stone into shaped recesses in a stone surface. The pieces are arranged to form designs, frequently flowers, leaves and other ornamental patterns.

The crucial feature is that different stones are set into the surface. The result is not simply paint applied over stone, nor is it an opening cut through a screen.

Pietra dura became especially prominent in Mughal architecture under Shah Jahan. At the Taj Mahal, coloured-stone inlay forms floral designs against the white marble. The Red Fort in Delhi also contains important examples of inlay decoration.

Calligraphy, geometry and relief carving

  • Calligraphy: Decorative writing. Inscriptions, including Quranic passages, are found on several mosques and tombs.
  • Geometric ornament: Repeated lines, polygons, stars and interlocking shapes used on screens, walls and floors.
  • Relief carving: A design carved so that its forms project from or remain recessed within the background surface.
  • Stucco: Decorative plasterwork used to form or finish surface designs.
  • Tile decoration: Glazed or coloured tiles used to cover and embellish architectural surfaces.

Floral arabesques, geometric patterns and calligraphic bands could appear together on the same building. Likewise, a jali might contain an arabesque pattern, while an arabesque might be executed through pietra dura. These terms describe different aspects of the ornament and are therefore not mutually exclusive.

Design, object and technique: Arabesque names a decorative design; jali names a perforated screen; pietra dura names an inlay technique. A single monument can use all 3.

Prelims focus

  • Arabesque refers to flowing, interlaced plant-like ornamental patterns.
  • Jali refers to a perforated lattice or screen.
  • Pietra dura uses coloured stones fitted into a prepared stone surface.
  • Calligraphy is decorative writing, often used for architectural inscriptions.
  • Sidi Saiyyed Mosque in Ahmedabad, completed in 1573, is famous for its tree-of-life jali.
  • Trap: Pietra dura is inlay, not another name for perforated stonework.

[Sources: NCERT, An Introduction to Indian Art, Part I, Class 11, Chapter 8, pp. 111, 120–121, and Glossary, pp. 126–130; NCERT, Our Pasts–II, Class 7, Chapter 5, Rulers and Buildings, p. 69; Ahmedabad Municipal Corporation, Heritage City, Sidi Saiyyed Mosque, monument description, accessed 23 November 2026; UNESCO World Heritage Centre, Taj Mahal, Outstanding Universal Value, accessed 23 November 2026.]

pictures.alt: Arabesque is a flowing plant design, jali is a pierced stone screen, and pietra dura is stone inlay; all can coexist in one monument.
pictures.caption: Three important decorative terms describe different things: a pattern, a perforated screen and a stone-inlay technique.

title: Arabesque, Jali, Pietra Dura and Other Architectural Decoration
